name: Sodium picosulfate
mechanism: Prodrug activated by colonic bacteria to form active metabolite (bis-(p-hydroxyphenyl)-pyridyl-2-methane - BHPM). Stimulates colonic peristalsis, inhibits water/electrolyte absorption, stimulates colonic mucosa. Onset 6-12h orally, 10-30 min rectally
dosing: Constipation: 5-10mg PO at bedtime (start 5mg). Bowel prep (pre-colonoscopy): Picolax sachets - 1 sachet (10mg) at 8am and 6pm day before procedure (each dissolved in 150ml water). Paediatric: 1 month-4 years: 2.5mg; 4-12 years: 2.5-5mg; >12 years: adult dose. Short-term use only
contraindications: Intestinal obstruction, ileus, acute abdomen (appendicitis, etc.), inflammatory bowel disease (active), severe dehydration, hereditary fructose intolerance (contains sorbitol in some formulations). Avoid long-term use
interactions: Diuretics ↑ hypokalaemia risk. Corticosteroids ↑ hypokalaemia. Cardiac glycosides (digoxin) - hypokalaemia enhances toxicity. Antibiotics may reduce efficacy (destroy activating bacteria)
monitoring: Ensure adequate hydration, especially with bowel prep. Electrolytes if prolonged use (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia). Abuse potential in eating disorders. Frequency of bowel movements. Watch for dependency
pregnancy: Limited data but no evidence of harm. Use if needed - dietary/lifestyle measures first-line. Not absorbed systemically in significant amounts. Generally considered safe
sideEffects: Common: abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, nausea, dizziness (especially with bowel prep - dehydration). Prolonged use: hypokalaemia, electrolyte imbalance, colonic atony (cathartic colon - loses normal function), dependency. Rare: angioedema, rash
pharmacokinetics: Minimal systemic absorption. Prodrug hydrolyzed by colonic bacteria to active BHPM. Onset: 6-12h orally (overnight), 10-30 min rectally. Acts locally in colon. Minimal enterohepatic circulation. Excreted in faeces
clinicalPearls: Brand: Dulcolax (tablets), Picolax (bowel prep sachets - contains sodium picosulfate + magnesium citrate). Similar mechanism to bisacodyl. Used short-term for constipation or bowel prep. NOT for chronic constipation - risk of dependency and 'cathartic colon'. First-line: lifestyle (fluid, fibre, exercise), then bulk-forming laxatives, then osmotic laxatives. Stimulants (picosulfate, bisacodyl, senna) are rescue therapy. Bowel prep: Picolax commonly used pre-colonoscopy - warn patients about frequency of loose stools, need to stay near toilet, clear fluids only. Adequate hydration critical during bowel prep (risk of dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, AKI). Split-dose regimen (evening before + morning of) better tolerated than same-day. Avoid long-term: risk of hypokalaemia, colon atony, melanosis coli (benign pigmentation), dependency. In opioid-induced constipation: consider peripherally-acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists (naloxegol) instead. Not absorbed: safe in pregnancy/breastfeeding (though lifestyle/bulk-forming preferred). May take 6-12h - advise to take at bedtime for morning effect
indication: Short-term relief of constipation. Bowel preparation before colonoscopy/surgery
